greeting.text: Corse is standing at the window with his hands behind his back, watching the crane. "Three years," he says, without turning round. "Nine sheets. Four hundred and eleven days of chain-work." He turns. He is not angry. "It will be done again. I have already written for a chainman. What I would like to know — and you may refuse, and I shall not press it — is whether you thought that would stop anything, or whether you knew it would not and did it regardless. Both are respectable. They are just different sorts of person."

"Eleven hundred people now know what their roofs were entered at," Corse says. He offers you the chair, as he always does. "I have had four letters from Rivermark this week. Two ask me to confirm the figure. One offers to sell me a mill at rather more than the figure. One is from a woman who would like to know whether her name is written anywhere, and I have replied that it is not, and that this is not a comfort and she should not take it as one."

greeting.text: "You found it, then," Corse says, and does not ask which figure or pretend not to know. He moves the chair out for you. "Sit. There is a ham and you have walked eleven miles."

"You shut the press," Corse says. He is not disappointed and he is not relieved and he is certainly not surprised. "About a third do. I have never once thought less of anybody for it and I have thought a great deal about why the other two thirds do not sleep afterwards."

Corse waits, comfortably, for as long as it takes. He does not fill the silence, and it becomes apparent quite quickly that he could sit there until dark.

what_i_buy.text: "Grain forward at spring price. Debt paper at a discount against the term. Water rights where they are severable, which is rarely. Quarry writs. Carriage. Some wool, badly, once." "That is by area. By value it is less than it sounds, because a great deal of it is hill. I would not want you to leave thinking I had bought something impressive."

who_for.text: "The house," Corse says. "Which is a way of saying eleven people in three towns who have money in it and one of whom I have met." He turns his pen around on the desk. "I am a factor. A factor buys with somebody else's money on somebody else's instruction and takes a fortieth. If you are hoping I will produce a man in a black coat with a plan, I am afraid the answer is a list of subscribers and a quarterly meeting I am not invited to."

interjections.text: Aldric: "Then who gives the instruction?" Corse, without any edge at all: "The meeting, brother. That is what a meeting is."

the_instruction.text: "I do," Corse says, "within a figure. They give me a figure and a year and I spend it as well as I can, and I am judged on the return and on nothing else whatever." He says this without pride and without apology. "It is why I am able to answer you. There is no secret in it. There is only a figure, and I am under it, and I shall be under it again next year."

choices.label: And nobody ever asks what it is for?

for_is_not_a_question.text: "For," Corse repeats, as though turning over a coin somebody has handed him. "You will find that it is not a question that comes up. A field is bought because it is cheap and next to another field. A debt is bought because it is discounted. Nobody sits down and decides to own a valley. It simply turns out, at the end of a good enough run of ordinary purchases, that somebody does."

interjections.text: Sera does not say anything. She is looking at him the way you look at a mirror that has just shown you something behind you.

he_agrees_pleasantly.text: "Very likely," Corse agrees. "I should be interested to meet them. I have written to the meeting twice asking what the works at the head of the valley are ultimately for, and been answered both times with a revised figure and a request for a fuller return." He shrugs, once, minutely. "I stopped asking. That is not a confession. It is a description of employment."

the_mark_question.text: "The bob and the square," he says, and finds a note in the desk and holds it up. "It is the house's mark. It has been the house's mark since my grandfather, who was a surveyor before he was anything else and thought a merchant's arms were vulgar." He puts it back. "We stamp it on everything we own or have measured, which is why you have been seeing it. It is not a signal to anybody. It is the equivalent of writing your name in a book."

the_plate.text: "That would be the Fenmoor lot," Corse says, and thinks, and is quite untroubled. "We bought a bankrupt armourer's stock four years ago because it was cheap, and sold it on at Greyhythe because it was not our trade. Where it went after that I could not tell you, and I did not ask, and you are entirely right that I should have." A pause. "I shall not pretend to be surprised. Sold goods go where the price is."

somebody_did.text: "Somebody sold to somebody who sold to somebody," Corse says. "That is not the same sentence and the difference is the whole of commerce. I can give you the name of the man at Greyhythe who took the stock off me. He will give you a name. It will go four or five deep and then it will stop with a carter who is dead." He looks at you steadily. "I am not saying that to close the subject. I am saying it because it is what will happen and I would rather you spent the winter on something else."

the_stone.text: "Then a surveyor of ours has been down there," Corse says, "which I would expect, because we hold that ground and a man does not sign for ground he has not walked." He turns the pen around again. "The workings under the old quarry are ours. They are lawful, they are on our own land, and there is no permit in this county for digging on your own ground because nobody ever thought one would be needed."

interjections.text: Ilse: "There are three thousand goblins living on top of your workings and they are being pushed up onto my road." Corse writes that down. He actually writes it down.

he_does_not_know_either.text: "Stone," Corse says. "That is what is on the return and that is what I am costing it as." I am instructed to continue and to keep the works fully manned, and I do, because that is what a factor does with an instruction he thinks is poor."

interjections.text: Sera: "He does not know. He genuinely does not know, and he has told us he does not know, and it has made everything worse."

why_rivermark.text: "It is where the road is," Corse says. "Everything at the head of that valley has to come down past the town or go forty miles round. "I am aware that is a poor thing to say about eleven hundred people. It is nevertheless why the house is interested and I would be lying if I dressed it."

he_does_not_answer_that_one.text: "That is a question about the future," Corse says, "and I have made it a rule not to guess in front of people who will remember what I guessed." he_sees_you_out.text: He comes to the door with you, tells you which way the towpath is less mud, and says that if you think of anything on the road you are to come back rather than write, because letters take a fortnight and he would rather have the conversation. the_second_visit_is_easier.text: "Most people find the second visit easier," Corse says, without a scrap of condescension. "The first one you spend working out that I am going to answer. Come back when you have a question that costs you something to ask. Those are the only ones I enjoy."

And a total, in a column, between a weir and a stand of oak, added up by somebody paid by the day to add things up. It is less than the crane on the new landing cost. Nothing about it is cruel. Nobody wrote it to be cruel. That is the part you are going to be carrying about for a while.

Do not agree yet — read the second sheet first, and note that there is no clause about ending it, and that nobody has ever asked for one."

He is recording you: that you did it in front of him, and how long you took to decide, and whether your hand was steady.

it_changes_nothing.text: "You have a record of what the ground is worth," Corse says. "What you have actually taken is the only copy on which somebody wrote a word in the margin without thinking. That is worth something. It is only not worth what you have been hoping."

the_word_clearance.text: "It is a head in a column," Corse says. "Everything that has to be paid for and removed before ground is worth its valuation goes under it. A hedge. A weir. A stand of oak." He does not look away and he does not soften it. "Yes. And a town, if a town is in the way, and the figure beside it is not what it would cost to kill anybody, it is what it would cost to buy them out and move them, and it has been revised downward twice because the second time somebody costed it properly. That is the honest answer and I am sorry it is not a worse one."

interjections.text: Aldric: "Move them where?" Corse: "That would be under a different head, brother, and it has not been costed, because nobody has asked for it yet."

he_explains_and_it_helps_nothing.text: He explains it. nothing_at_all.text: "Nothing at all," Corse says. "That is the point of a retainer. there_is_no_out.text: "There is no out," Corse says, kindly. "Not because I would prevent it — I would not, and you may burn the articles this afternoon. There is no out because the fact of it is that you took it, and I know, and you know I know, and there is no document anywhere that can be torn up to make that stop being so." He drinks. "It really is a remarkably economical instrument."

then_we_understand.text: "Then we understand each other," Corse says, and writes it down, because he writes everything down. "I shall tell you what happens next, since you will find out anyway. The house will want a name. I shall be asked for one, and I shall give the true answer, which is that I do not know. That will not be believed, and a man will come up from downriver who is not a factor and does not answer questions." He looks up. "That is not a threat. It is a schedule."

he_expected_nothing.text: "I expected precisely this," Corse says. "A town that knows what it is worth is a town that sells sooner and argues less, and I have written to the meeting to say so, because it would be dishonest of me to let them think you had cost us anything." For the first time there is something under the evenness — not anger. Something more like regret at being understood too late. "You did the right thing. I want to be clear that I am saying so, and that it did not work."

choices.label: It worked for them. They know.

he_grants_it.text: "They know," Corse agrees. "That is not nothing. In nineteen years it is the only thing anybody has ever taken off me that I could not put back." He turns his pen around on the desk. "Come back in the spring. There will be more to say by then and I would rather say it to you than to whoever they send."

a_bad_quarter.text: "At a good deal more than that," Corse says, "it stops being mine." He says it exactly as he says everything. "Understand what I am: I am a man with a district and a figure I am answerable for. While the loss is a figure I can carry, the whole of it is between you and me and I will go on giving you the chair and the ham. When it is not, it goes downriver in the quarter's return, and men who have never walked this valley read it against eleven others and decide what is to be done about the valley that is losing money." He turns his glass. "They are not cruel. They have never seen it. That is very much worse and I have watched it happen twice."

he_has_not_decided.text:
"Whether to write back," Corse says. "That is all it is. There is no other decision available to me and I would not want you to leave here thinking there was." He looks at the window and the crane beyond it. "If I write back, I am a factor who argues with the house about four people who walked here, and I have precisely one of those letters in me and I have been saving it for eleven years. If I do not, it is done in the ordinary way by ordinary people and nobody in it will ever have met you."

He turns back.

"I am telling you because you have never once lied to me in this room, and I find I mind about that. Do not mistake it for an alliance. I would like you to leave the valley."
